title: Computational Complexity of Locating the Kostochka–Pyber Non-Planar Subgraph

problemStatement.formal: Given a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with $|E(G)| \ge n^{1+\varepsilon}$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, Kostochka–Pyber (1988) guarantees a non-planar $H \subseteq G$ with $|V(H)| \le C_\varepsilon = O_\varepsilon(1)$. What is the time complexity of an algorithm that outputs such an $H$? Equivalently, is there an algorithm running in time $f(\varepsilon)\cdot\mathrm{poly}(n)$ that returns a vertex set $S$ with $|S| \le C_\varepsilon$ and $G[S]$ non-planar?
problemStatement.plain: Kostochka and Pyber proved that any graph with n^(1+ε) edges must contain a non-planar piece on only a bounded number C_ε of vertices, regardless of how large the graph is. Their proof shows such a piece exists but does not obviously produce it efficiently. This problem asks how computationally hard it is to actually find one of these small non-planar subgraphs: can it be done in polynomial time in n for each fixed ε, or is locating the obstruction genuinely harder than knowing it exists?
whyMatters: Separates existence from construction — a recurring theme (algorithmic Local Lemma, constructive Ramsey bounds) where non-constructive guarantees were later matched by efficient algorithms.

Making the guarantee constructive would turn a pure existence theorem into a certified subroutine and link topological obstruction theory (Kuratowski, K5/K3,3 subdivisions) to the algorithmic theory of topological-minor testing.
